title: Three-figure bearings
log: 2026-11-01T08:04:34Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: Neither bank point teaches three-figure true bearings used with the sine and cosine rules in navigation problems; both only define bearings or convert compass bearings and elevation, so the sine and cosine rule step would be a new idea rather than a small change.

draft.title: Three-figure bearings
card: A bearing is a direction measured clockwise from north. It is written with three figures and a T, such as 045°T or 135°T.
North is 000°T, east is 090°T, south is 180°T and west is 270°T.
To find the back bearing, add 180° if the bearing is under 180°, or subtract 180° if it is over. Example: if B is on 070°T from A, then A is on 250°T from B.

In navigation problems, draw a north line at each point. North lines are parallel, so they give equal alternate angles. This lets you find angles inside the triangle, then use the sine or cosine rule.
draft.remember: Measure clockwise from north, and swap direction by adding or subtracting 180°.

a.q: A hiker walks from camp to a lookout on a bearing of 125°T. What is the bearing from the lookout back to camp?
a.why: The bearing is under 180°, so add 180°: 125° + 180° = 305°T. The answer 055°T comes from subtracting from 180° instead.
a.clue: The return direction is exactly opposite.

b.q: A ship sails from P to Q on a bearing of 070°T, then from Q to R on a bearing of 150°T. What is the interior angle PQR?
b.why: The bearing from Q back to P is 070° + 180° = 250°T. The angle between 250°T and 150°T is 100°. The angle 80° is how far the ship turns, not the angle inside the triangle.
b.clue: Find the back bearing from Q to P first.

check.summary: No problems found. Both answers check out: 125° + 180° = 305°T, and the angle between the back bearing 250°T and 150°T is 100°.
